extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Philosophical Transactions: natural philosophers, anatomists, astronomers, instrument-makers and physicians (17th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and documenting anatomical dissections, physiological experiments, instrument descriptions, and astronomical observations with observational detail, experimental demonstration, and technical method. Includes how-to use instruments and how to present supporting evidence from injections, ligatures, microscopy, long-term observations, and measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prune superfluous non-bearing branches before spring
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘not only suckers, but all superfluous not-bearing branches are to be carefully cut away before, or at, the entrance of the spring.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale given: suckers rob fruit because until the whole tree is filled with sap the fruit cannot be served in the uttermost branches; pruning removes branches that compete for sap and thus protects fruiting. Surrounding discussion links pruning timing to sap pulsion, and to avoiding interference with yearly shoots and uppermost growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess effects of drawing sap from trees
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘it seems probable, that drawing sap constantly from trees every year, will not hinder their growth in body, branches, leaves, nor fruit, to any great prejudice; … If plenty of sap drawn from trees hinder at all, it seems probable, that it will hinder growth of fruit, leaves, or uppermost shoots in tops of trees, and yearly shoots in extreme parts.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative guidance: weigh pulsion supplying emptied pores until capacity is filled; compare to persons who grow fatter by often bleeding; consider side-effects on highest shoots and fruit. Also note environmental factors (sunny/south side roots run longer sap; cold rain over-cooling hinders sap pulsion and digestion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate cardiac circulation by experiments on living animals
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘he shows, by experiments made on living animals, that the motion of the heart is performed by the contraction of its muscular fibres; that the auricles contract first, and thereby propel the blood into the ventricles; then the ventricles contract, whereby the blood is driven into the arteries; being prevented from returning into the auricles by the situation and connexion of the valves.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental standards cited: use observations of sequential contractions; perform ligature experiments (tie the great artery and observe veins empty; pass a ligature round the vena cava where it joins the right auricle and observe immediate distension) to infer flow direction; use anatomical analysis of valve position to argue prevention of backflow; combine physiological observation with mechanical demonstration for convincing proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish pulmonary (lung) site for arterial-venous communication
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He demonstrates that the last-mentioned communication takes place in the lungs.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning invoked: because more blood is sent into arteries than is required for nourishment, the superfluous blood must return by veins; anatomical/experimental evidence (including ligature experiments and observations of pulmonary structure) is used to show exchanges occur in the lungs. The criterion is to locate and demonstrate the actual site of arterial-to-venous communication rather than relying on speculative pores or anastomoses elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use injection and microscopy to reveal glandular structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods described: injecting through the emulgent artery a black liquor mixed with spirit of wine; cutting the kidneys longways; using the microscope to observe kidneys and find them 'a congeries of small glands... like little apples appendant to the sanguineous vessels'; syringing air into the spleen to make it turgid and, after exsiccation and cutting, observe membranous cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical methodological guidance for anatomical/histological demonstration: use colored/marked injections to trace connections between vessels and glandular structures; perform longitudinal cuts to reveal spatial relations; employ the microscope for fine structure; inflate organs (syringing air) to reveal membrane/cell architecture; use exsiccation followed by sectioning to visualize cell-like cavities. These combined techniques are presented as necessary evidence to support structural and functional claims about organs (kidneys, spleen, brain cortex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate organ structure with proposed physiological function
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: liver 'separates the gall, which being conveyed into the intestines, he asserts to be subservient to digestion'; cortex of brain as 'a congeries of glands' separating particles for sensation; spleen designed 'for a new separation and mixture of the juices' contributing to bile formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: base functional inferences on observed microstructure and anatomical connections. The author evaluates organ function by (a) reviewing prior opinions, (b) presenting new microscopic/anatomical observations, and (c) offering modest, evidence-linked hypotheses about use (e.g., secretion, separation, conveyance into other organs). Emphasize humility and comparison with existing literature when proposing functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe instrument construction and step-by-step use for reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed description of a perspective-drawing instrument: parts (sight A with arm B, cylinder CD, piece ED moving round centre E, frame SSSS, ruler HH with strings aaa bbb and counterpoise QQ, pen I attached by brass handle V) and operation: 'Set the instrument on a table, and fix the sight A at any height above the table, and at any distance from the frame you please. Then, looking through the sight A, and holding the pen I in your hand, move the head of the pin P up and down the outlines of the object, and the point I will describe, on the paper... the shape of the object so traced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: User-facing guidance: provide both mechanical description (how pulleys, counterweights and sliding rulers maintain horizontality and steadiness) and procedural steps for use (setup, sighting, motion of pin and pen). The description functions as both construction specification and reproducibility protocol for other makers/users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose and verify astronomical tables from long-term precise observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cassini 'composed certain tables, after 15 years observations made with exactness of the motion of the said satellites... These tables are contained in this book; and for verifying them, he has added the Ephemerides of those stars for the year lately elapsed, viz. An. 1668.' Also: observers used 'a telescope of 21 feet' and 'the inclination of the great diameter of the oval to the equator was measured several ways'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards for astronomical evidence: accumulate long-term (multi-year) precise observations before tabulating motions; include ephemerides for verification against recent observations; use instruments of adequate focal length/resolution; measure key angles by multiple independent methods to ensure consistency and to test theoretical hypotheses (e.g., ring hypothesis for Saturn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical exposition should provide general methods, particular constructions, and analytic justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary of Mesolabium: gives 'general methods for finding two means, by a circle and either an hyperbola or ellipsis', 'particular effections for finding out one or both of the means', gives analysis/algebra explaining how methods were invented, includes constructions for cubic and biquadratic equations, trisection of an angle, and general constructions for solid problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for valuing mathematical contributions: present both general frameworks and particular worked constructions; supply algebraic/analytic foundations for geometric constructions; show how methods resolve classical problems (doubling the cube, cubic equations, trisection) and demonstrate breadth by giving constructions that handle families of problems rather than isolated cases. Clarity in methodology and demonstration of multiple independent solutions are highlighted as strengths.
